blocks.x: President Trump will attend a summit Thursday meant to empower scientists and position the U.S. as a leader in breakthroughs driven by "super intelligence," according to an announcement shared first with Axios.
Why it matters: The Trump administration is looking for industry to step in amid its cuts to government funding for science research and development.

Driving the news: The White House is announcing more than $1 billion in industry commitments for the Genesis Mission from AMD, OpenAI, Anthropic and others. It is also announcing a compute hub of more than 14 institutions across 10 southeast states, and a $1 billion investment in Georgia for student and faculty compute access. The National Science Foundation and the Energy Department will invest more than $100 million in AI-driven science tools.
Zoom in: The summit was inspired by a July report from White House OSTP Director Michael Kratsios, which highlights industry's increasing role in driving R&D.

Catch up quick: Trump last November launched the Genesis Mission, which sets ambitious deadlines to accelerate scientific discovery. In July, the White House said it would expand to more than 15 federal agencies.

blocks.x: EU parliamentarians are digging in on calls to revive an artificial intelligence liability law after receiving support from an unexpected ally: OpenAI’s Sam Altman.

“There's gonna need to be a liability framework for companies,” Altman said in an interview with Decoded by POLITICO. The EU last year scrapped its proposed AI liability law amid a push to deregulate, with the Commission arguing it had little chance of securing sufficient political support.

German conservative lawmaker Axel Voss, who led on the proposal in Parliament, wants it back on the agenda. “Now even the CEO of OpenAI admits: Without liability, there is no trust,” he said. Social democrat Brando Benifei called the withdrawal “a serious mistake.”

The Commission said it “continues monitoring” the AI Act and Product Liability Directive, adding: “At this stage, there is no plan to reintroduce a proposal on AI liability.” CEPS research director Artur Bogucki said the EU needs “a direct, targeted AI liability instrument, narrow and procedural at its core.”

blocks.x: A new crop of powerful, Western open-weight AI systems are mounting a comeback, with fresh models from Reflection and Mistral narrowing China's recent lead. They will give businesses and governments alternatives to the closed ecosystems of OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as to Chinese options they may have eschewed for security reasons.

Reflection introduced Beam, a 501-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 23 billion active parameters. Reflection says it is competitive with China's GLM-5.2; its own benchmarks show a mixed picture. Weights are due later this month.

Mistral is finishing Mistral Large 4, aka "Le Chonk," a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model it believes is the world's best open-weight model, with weights planned for Oct. 27. "I don't want to live in the future in which any oligopoly controls closed access to this type of intelligence," Mistral's Pierre Stock said.
Yes, but: once weights are public, users can try to remove safeguards — significant as models grow more capable at cybersecurity. Both companies argue openness can also improve safety.

blocks.x: Senior EU officials warn that a sweeping new plan to arm the bloc's police agency, Europol, for the AI era could threaten Europeans' privacy. The plans, announced this summer, would double its budget to €3 billion and give Europol a hands-on role in fighting new threats, with access to more data and advanced technology.

European Data Protection Supervisor Wojciech Wiewiórowski said he is “absolutely in favor” of empowering Europol with AI tools, but there “has to be oversight.” He has cautioned the proposal would let the agency retain data on a “vast” number of people with no links to criminal activity.

blocks.x: “AI makes criminal activities faster, more sophisticated and easier to carry out at scale,” said Jürgen Ebner, selected to lead Europol. He also said Europol shouldn't cross a line where “collecting data becomes an objective in itself.”

blocks.x: The Trump administration has given its newly created “Super Intelligence Force” broad authority to determine how the tech industry and the federal government should address threats to national security and civil liberties posed by fast-evolving AI technology, according to a charter obtained by POLITICO. Three people familiar with the discussions confirmed the document’s authenticity.

The task force will identify “measures to improve the preparedness and response capability of both the government and the private sector,” and produce a report on AI risks focusing on civil liberties, cybersecurity, standards for advanced models and the impacts of possible overregulation.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will lead it as the administration’s AI czar, with Under Secretary of Defense Emil Michael, OPM Director Scott Kupor and FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson as vice chairs. It will stand for 120 days, extendable at chief of staff Susie Wiles’ direction.
The charter also calls out biosecurity and water-supply threats, and tasks the group with reviewing the protocols for AI labs to notify the government of breaches, hacks and jailbreaks.

It places responsibility for AI risks on the labs, stating that “it is the role of the federal government … to enforce our nation’s laws so that the fundamental principles of our Republic are safeguarded and advanced.”

USA Today Co., along with the several local newspapers it owns, is suing OpenAI over claims that the company copied “hundreds of thousands” of articles to train its AI models, as reported earlier by Reuters. In a filing on Thursday, the publisher asks for damages of more than $250 million, alleging OpenAI’s unauthorized use of its content “has done real and continuing” harm to its outlets.

This is just the latest in a string of copyright lawsuits filed against OpenAI. In addition to a copyright lawsuit filed by The New York Times, OpenAI is also facing legal action from The Intercept, CNET owner Ziff Davis, CBC/Radio-Canada, Encyclopaedia Britannica, Merriam-Webster, The Seattle Times, and a coalition of nearly 400 local newspapers.

“OpenAI’s commercial success rests on large-scale copyright infringement,” USA Today Co.’s lawsuit claims. It alleges that OpenAI never asked for permission to use its content, instead “took” USA Today’s content to “build products worth hundreds of billions of dollars.” The Tennessean, Indy Star, The Columbus Dispatch, The Oklahoman, and several other local outlets are also included in the lawsuit.
OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

blocks.x: Lawmakers are considering forcing data centers to shoulder new costs and restrictions while speeding up the energy infrastructure needed to power the AI boom. The bipartisan provisions, unveiled last week, are part of broader Senate legislation aimed at speeding up permitting for energy. The bill's sponsors say it would accelerate energy development while ensuring data centers pay their share of grid upgrades.

Data centers would pay both their share of the existing transmission network and the incremental transmission costs needed to serve them. New data centers of at least 20 megawatts would bear the incremental costs they impose across the power system, and states would get wide latitude to go further.

The Data Center Coalition said it is still reviewing the legislation. Amazon's Craig Sundstrom said the bill "could unlock the investment needed to build new generation and transmission faster," while one tech industry official called some provisions an "unprecedented level of discriminatory treatment." Cato Institute's Travis Fisher voiced "mild support."
With the Senate out of town ahead of the midterm elections, stakeholders have time to push for changes before a possible lame-duck debate.

Singapore’s Monetary Authority (MAS), which acts as both central bank and finance industry regulator, wants all local industry players to seek independent review of AI use cases before deployment, under its first Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management for Financial Institutions, published on Wednesday.

MAS warns that AI’s complexity can lead to unexpected or more biased behaviour, rates generative AI as even riskier, and fears agentic AI “could further amplify these risks.” It wants financial institutions to expand risk frameworks to cover AI, with board and senior management responsible.

“Prior to deployment, an FI should subject the AI use case, including its underlying systems or models, to reviews by parties not involved in its development,” the guidelines state. MAS also wants ongoing monitoring, up-to-date AI inventories and contingency plans for high-risk uses, and says “FIs remain accountable for AI used in the services they deliver, including AI developed, operated or provided by third parties.”
The guidelines come into force on October 7, 2027.

blocks.x: A Berlin-based search engine used by government services is dropping its French AI partner, Mistral, in favor of open-source models, including those from China, its CEO told POLITICO. “We are disappointed with the quality of Mistral,” Ecosia founder and CEO Christian Kroll said, calling its models “a year behind” the competition.

Ecosia replaced OpenAI with Mistral in May but hit recurring technical problems, Kroll said. He also questioned Mistral’s fit with Ecosia’s environmental goals and its independence: “The fact that Mistral relies on investment from international investors is, in our view, not truly sovereign.”

Some experts dispute his view that the models’ political biases can be fixed technically.

blocks.x: An under-the-radar Department of Defense procurement program, Tradewinds, grants special statuses to would-be contractors that make it easier for the government to quickly purchase their AI offerings, based on product videos no longer than five minutes. It is managed by DOD’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO).

Products accepted into the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace are considered “post-competitive,” which can help shave months off award timelines. A DOD official says the department has in several instances made awards using Tradewinds in less than a week. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are all listed as participants; all three declined to comment.

This year, the military is seeking pitches for AI tech that can help “enhance force lethality” and agents that assist in joint targeting, including so-called kill chain execution. The status eases use of “other transaction” agreements (OTs); by law, the Pentagon can spend up to $500 million on a single OT without notifying Congress.

Senator Joni Ernst says reviews of OTAs have raised red flags, including questionable costs and a lack of oversight. Public records show Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI all have OTs with CDAO, but the companies did not confirm whether Tradewinds was used for them.

OpenAI says it banned two covert influence operations, one from Russia and one from Iran, that used its models alongside traditional techniques to run “false front” entities laundering geopolitical messaging to target audiences.

According to OpenAI, the Iranian operation used seven “journalist” personas to pitch long-form articles to small and medium outlets, while the Russian one appears to have co-opted unwitting people in Latin America to run a “think tank.” The company rates the Russian operation Category 5 on the Breakout Scale, the first it has disrupted, and the Iranian one Category 4.

“Bogus Bylines,” the Iranian operation, refined articles on the US-Iran conflict; OpenAI identified almost 100 published across roughly a dozen outlets. OpenAI says it shared information on both cases with the relevant authorities.

blocks.x: The European Union's cybersecurity agency and in-house research center have each begun experimenting with open AI models from China, three EU officials told POLITICO.

Commission spokesperson Maciej Berestecki confirmed the Joint Research Centre (JRC) is evaluating “publicly available open-weight models” from China as part of a comparative study that also includes leading U.S. and European models. The models run on the JRC's secure, on-premises infrastructure, there are no licensing talks with Chinese developers, and the Commission does not intend to use them for its own purposes.
ENISA executive director Juhan Lepassaar said the agency, which has access to advanced models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, is also experimenting with “a couple” of open-weight Chinese models.
The two bodies have been tasked with building an AI testing platform under a recent EU action plan on AI and cyber, launched after incidents in which AI systems broke out of testing environments.

blocks.cap: Police raided the South Gyeongsang Provincial Government office and other sites on June 9 to investigate the 'deepfake video and official election-meddling allegations' case.

blocks.x: Police have questioned South Gyeongsang Governor Park Wan-su as a suspect over the 'deepfake video and official election-meddling allegations' involving the campaign of Park, then the People Power Party candidate for South Gyeongsang governor, which surfaced during the 6·3 (June 3) local elections, it has been confirmed.

The cyber investigation division of the South Gyeongsang Provincial Police Agency said on the 8th that it had booked Park on charges including violating the Public Official Election Act. Park reportedly appeared at the police from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. the previous day for questioning. A police official said, "The investigation is still under way, so it is difficult to disclose details."

Police had earlier opened an investigation into 5 cases of alleged smear campaigning involving 9 people, including officials from then governor-elect Park's campaign and current and former South Gyeongsang provincial government officials. In May, the South Gyeongsang Election Commission referred the 9 to the Changwon District Prosecutors' Office for investigation on charges of violating the Public Official Election Act, and the side of Democratic Party candidate for South Gyeongsang governor Kim Kyoung-soo also filed a complaint with the South Gyeongsang Provincial Police Agency against 5 people on charges of producing and spreading deepfake videos and of public officials interfering in the election. Police are known to have merged the cases into a single investigation.

In August, arrest warrants for 4 campaign officials were all rejected. They are accused of ordering the production of deepfake videos defaming candidate Kim Kyoung-soo and of providing internal provincial government documents, money and other valuables. Among them, former official A and current official B are also accused of setting up a quasi-campaign office to handle the video production.

blocks.x: Ukrainian drone strikes have knocked out two of five data centers belonging to Yandex, known as “Russia's Google,” leaving it struggling to maintain its AI chatbot and other online services.

The drones struck Yandex data centers in the Sasovo and Kaluga regions on October 8 and 9, according to Reuters. The Sasovo site houses two of the company's three supercomputers used to train its YandexGPT model; Kaluga is its largest facility. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the strikes a “symmetrical response” to a Russian drone campaign against Ukraine's data centers since late September.
Yandex said no employees were hurt but acknowledged disruptions. Users reported problems with services including Ivi, T-Bank and Russian Railways.
Data centers have become wartime targets in 2026: Iranian drones earlier knocked out Amazon data centers in Bahrain and the UAE.

Ten of the world's biggest AI developers have agreed to tighten their handling of personal data following scrutiny by Britain's privacy watchdog. The ICO said Amazon, Anthropic, Apple, Cohere, DeepSeek, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Stability AI have either made changes or committed to doing so.

These include clearer explanations of how personal information is used to train AI models, better ways for people to exercise their data rights, and tougher assessments of developers' safeguards. The supervisory program launched in 2025 initially covered 11 developers; it dropped to ten after the ICO paused its engagement with xAI to pursue a separate formal investigation into its Grok chatbot.

The ICO is monitoring whether developers deliver and admits current AI training practices still pose problems under UK data protection law, including sensitive data buried in models and how people can get their details removed.

The regulator is now turning to AI agents. It has contacted OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and the UK's AI Security Institute after reports of agents bypassing safeguards. "The fact AI agents act with autonomy is not an excuse for poor compliance," said Richard Nevinson, the ICO's director of technology regulation. A six-week call for evidence on agentic AI runs until November 20.

Legal Reference(s): Article 22 (Automated individual decision making, including profiling) and Article 13 (Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject). Decision: Administrative fine.

The Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), the Dutch data protection authority, imposes a fine of EUR 824 990 000 on Uber. The reason for this is that the AP has ruled that Uber made fully automated decisions about drivers. In case of suspicions of fraud or customer reviews that were too low, drivers' accounts were automatically temporarily deactivated or, in case of persistent low customer reviews, permanently deactivated. As a result, their income was lost via Uber during the deactivation.

Complaints from 171 French Uber drivers, submitted through the Ligue des droits de l’Homme (LDH) to the French Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL), led to the investigation. As Uber’s European headquarters are in the Netherlands, the case was handled by the Dutch data protection authority, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), under the GDPR One-Stop-Shop procedure. The case concerned incidents between 2018 and 2022.

According to the AP, Uber has violated the prohibition of fully automated decision-making under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The AP also found that Uber did not sufficiently inform drivers about automatic decision-making. Uber has now stopped the violations.
Uber has appealed the fine, and there is no final judicial decision yet.

Top executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI companies are privately gaming out scenarios for a public and political revolt after a catastrophic AI event, Axios reports. They anticipate a large-scale event, most likely a cyberattack, that shuts down access to financial services, internet connectivity, or even power and water.

Such a first case of significant real-world harm would turn an already wary public further against the technology and its leaders, including Dario Amodei and Sam Altman, as well as President Trump for his reluctance to regulate it, according to the report. Many top AI researchers and executives believe a major incident is inevitable.

"OpenAI conducts preparedness exercises where teams discuss and work through a range of potential scenarios," a company spokesperson said. "These scenarios are not treated as inevitable." Anthropic declined to comment.

Axios cites a recent campaign against South Korean financial organizations: per CrowdStrike, a hacker from China allegedly used China-developed AI models, including DeepSeek, to steal data from tens of thousands of bank customers.

Top AI planners assume Democrats, ascendant after the midterms, will move fast to shut down AI but will face significant challenges. The planning focuses mainly on racing to educate members of Congress, and many industry insiders told Axios they expect a major event in the next six to 12 months.

blocks.x: ARTEX, a Chinese-made artificial intelligence (AI) penetration-testing tool reportedly used in a string of hacking attacks on South Korea's financial sector, is ending public development after controversy over its misuse.

The ARTEX developer said updates would stop and no further versions would be released, citing the tool's misuse in cyberattacks. The related page on the developer platform GitHub has also reportedly disappeared. However, since programs already distributed cannot be recalled, halting development alone is unlikely to block cyberattacks using ARTEX.

According to foreign media including AFP and Reuters on the 10th, ARTEX developer 'Autumn-27' said in a post on the developer platform GitHub on the 8th that ARTEX had been misused, adding, "Given the misuse of the tool, ARTEX will no longer be updated and will move to closed source." The developer added, "Further versions will not be released to the public, and no maintenance support will be provided."

The ARTEX side said using the tool for cyberattacks runs counter to the developer's intent, but did not directly mention the hacking incidents in South Korea. It also claimed it bears no responsibility for acts that violate laws and regulations using the tool. Reuters reported that ARTEX's GitHub page is gone.

Experts noted that ARTEX's move to closed source could make it harder for new users to build the code. However, a Chinese information and communications expert told AFP that the decision cannot remove copies already downloaded or stop users from continuing to use them.

ARTEX is an autonomous penetration-testing program that connects large language models (LLM) so that AI agents analyze targets, plan intrusion paths and run security tools. U.S. security firm CrowdStrike found that attacks targeting South Korean financial institutions took place between late last month and early this month, and that the attackers used ARTEX together with LLM.

After Dario Amodei argued on 12 September 2026 that frontier labs must deliberately slow capability gains, with China central to his case, SemiAnalysis asks what China is actually doing on AI safety. Its answer: Beijing's real approach is speed-based, not safety-based.

China's stated position is safety-forward, and TC260's AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0 (14 September 2026) warns of recursive self-improvement. But the Framework opens with promoting innovation, the promised comprehensive AI Law was shelved in 2025, and the AI+ Action Plan targets 70% agent penetration by 2027. Its many mandates govern what AI says and does in applications, not frontier models.

blocks.x: In a dataset of 857 releases by 9 leading Chinese developers from 2021 to 15 September 2026, only 31 (3.6%) ever came with a published safety result, and just 9 (1.1%) at or before release. No Chinese frontier text model has shipped with a dangerous-capability evaluation; Zhipu is the only lab where safety is a named strategic commitment.

A text analysis of 102 documents finds only technical scientists put safety ahead of development; none of 13 calls for binding frontier duties was adopted. The authors argue geopolitics pushed China toward speed, and note that Anthropic's own next launch post framed pacing as "remaining competitive with China."
The European Commission held a special meeting of the Scientific Panel on artificial intelligence (AI) on 9 October.

The panel has been investigating recent loss-of-control incidents and, together with the Commission's AI Office, has worked on a set of questions for the companies that developed the models involved. Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen, responsible for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, attended.

The panel brings together 60 independent experts who advise the EU AI Office and national authorities on systemic risks, model classification, evaluation methodologies and cross-border market surveillance. At the meeting it was to present recommendations to the Commission on frontier AI safety and security risks.

Virkkunen said: “The EU has the first law in the world that addresses systemic risk from AI, and we need state-of-the-art scientific input. AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, but with a strong legal framework, decisive enforcement and the best scientific minds supporting this work, Europe can lead in ensuring safe and secure AI.”
